# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) results from the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium, leading to progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy, restrictive physiology, and heart failure [1]. Long considered rare and untreatable, CA is now recognized as an underdiagnosed yet increasingly manageable condition, owing to advances in noninvasive imaging and disease-modifying therapy [2]. The two predominant subtypes are light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, arising from clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, which may be hereditary (ATTRv) or wild-type (ATTRwt) [3].

## Epidemiology and Pathophysiology

ATTRwt amyloidosis is increasingly identified in elderly patients, particularly men, and is found in up to 13% of patients hospitalized with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [4]. It has also been detected in a substantial proportion of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis [5]. Hereditary ATTR is caused by pathogenic variants in the *TTR* gene; the Val122Ile variant is notably prevalent among individuals of West African ancestry [6]. AL amyloidosis carries the worst prognosis when cardiac involvement is present, reflecting the direct cardiotoxicity of circulating light chains in addition to fibril deposition [7].

The pathophysiology involves destabilization of the native protein, dissociation into amyloidogenic intermediates, and aggregation into insoluble fibrils [8]. In ATTR, age-related and genetic factors promote tetramer dissociation, while in AL, monoclonal free light chains drive both deposition and oxidative myocyte injury [9].

## Clinical Presentation

CA typically presents with progressive heart failure, often with preserved ejection fraction, and signs of right-sided congestion [10]. Extracardiac clues are important: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and spontaneous biceps tendon rupture frequently precede cardiac diagnosis in ATTR [11]. In AL amyloidosis, periorbital purpura, macroglossia, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and autonomic dysfunction may be present [12]. Disproportionate elevation in cardiac biomarkers and discordance between wall thickness on echocardiography and QRS voltage on electrocardiography are characteristic red flags [13].

## Diagnosis

Echocardiography typically demonstrates increased ventricular wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, and a characteristic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain [14]. Cardiac magnetic resonance reveals diffuse late gadolinium enhancement and elevated native T1 and extracellular volume, supporting the diagnosis [15]. A landmark advance has been the validation of bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy (technetium-pyrophosphate or DPD); grade 2–3 myocardial uptake in the absence of a monoclonal protein is highly specific for ATTR-CA and can obviate endomyocardial biopsy [16].

Critically, exclusion of a plasma cell dyscrasia with serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light-chain assays is mandatory before attributing scintigraphy findings to ATTR [17]. When AL is suspected or monoclonal protein is present, tissue confirmation with Congo red staining and proteomic typing by mass spectrometry remains the gold standard [18]. Endomyocardial biopsy retains near-100% sensitivity when noninvasive evaluation is inconclusive [19].

## Treatment

For ATTR-CA, the TTR stabilizer tafamidis was shown in the ATTR-ACT trial to reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations [20]. More recently, the gene-silencing agents patisiran and vutrisiran, which reduce hepatic TTR production, have demonstrated benefit; the HELIOS-B trial showed that vutrisiran reduced death and cardiovascular events in ATTR-CA [21,22]. Acoramidis, another oral stabilizer, improved outcomes in the ATTRibute-CM trial [23]. Investigational approaches including CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing have shown durable TTR knockdown [24].

AL amyloidosis treatment targets the underlying plasma cell clone. The addition of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab to bortezomib-based regimens significantly improved hematologic and organ responses in the ANDROMEDA trial [25]. Autologous stem cell transplantation remains an option for selected, low-risk patients [26]. Prognosis is stratified by validated staging systems incorporating troponin and natriuretic peptides [27].

Supportive heart failure management in CA differs from conventional approaches: loop diuretics are the mainstay, while neurohormonal antagonists and beta-blockers are often poorly tolerated owing to fixed stroke volume and autonomic dysfunction [28]. Anticoagulation is frequently warranted given the high prevalence of atrial thrombi, even in sinus rhythm [29]. Advanced therapies, including cardiac transplantation combined with disease-directed treatment, may benefit carefully selected patients [30].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has transformed from an orphan diagnosis into an actionable disease. Heightened clinical suspicion, recognition of extracardiac red flags, and judicious use of noninvasive imaging—particularly bone scintigraphy with mandatory exclusion of plasma cell dyscrasia—enable timely diagnosis. With multiple effective disease-modifying therapies now available for both ATTR and AL subtypes, early detection is paramount to improving outcomes.
